title: Sharp Wizard OZ-7000
subtitle: Transparent touch panel over swappable physical IC cards — a plug-and-play hardware UI before capacitive touch
why_scout_cares: The Sharp Wizard's defining interaction model is genuinely unique and was never replicated: a transparent touch-sensitive overlay panel sits above a recessed slot for swappable IC cards. Each card has a printed template visible through the glass, and 20 touch zones on the glass map to card-specific functions. Swapping the card physically changes what the device can do AND what buttons appear on its surface. This is hardware-defined modular UI — a plug-and-play interface paradigm distinct from software-based menus, capacitive touchscreens, or stylus input. No other artifact in the museum does this.

research.title: Sharp Wizard OZ-7000
research.overview:
The Sharp Wizard OZ-7000 was Sharp Corporation's first electronic organizer, launched in 1989. It bridged the world of pocket computers and the emerging PDA category, but its defining innovation was a transparent touch-sensitive overlay panel paired with swappable physical IC cards. Each IC card contained ROM software and a printed template visible through the glass; 20 touch zones on the overlay mapped to card-specific functions. The Wizard was commercially successful, spawning a product line that ran through the mid-1990s, and was immortalized in a 1998 Seinfeld episode ('The Wizard') where Jerry gives one to his father as a gift.

At 163 × 94 × 21.5 mm and powered by two coin cells, the OZ-7000 featured a 96×64 dot monochrome LCD (8 lines × 16 characters), 32 KB of non-volatile memory, a non-QWERTY custom keyboard layout, and a proprietary serial port for PC connectivity. The IC card slot predated the PCMCIA standard and was incompatible with it. Available cards included scientific calculator, thesaurus, 8-language translator, investment planner, spreadsheet (Lotus 1-2-3 compatible), games (Sokoban, Tetris, chess), and later a BASIC programming card. The US model was prefixed 'OZ' — a pun on The Wizard of Oz — while European and Asian models used the 'IQ' prefix.

deepDive.heading: The Transparent Touch Panel
deepDive.text: The OZ-7000's signature interaction model: a transparent plastic touch-sensitive overlay covering a recessed slot in the right-hand section of the device. The overlay registered touch across a 4×5 matrix of 20 zones — eight zones on each side and four along the bottom. When a user inserted an IC card into the slot behind the panel, the card's printed template (showing button labels, icons, or custom layouts) was visible through the glass. The device's firmware mapped each of the 20 touch zones to card-specific functions. Swapping the card immediately transformed not just the software but the visible input surface — a plug-and-play physical UI that predated capacitive touchscreens and app icons.

deepDive.heading: IC Card Ecosystem
deepDive.text: The IC cards contained ROM with application software plus a coordinate-to-function mapping table. Available cards included: OZ-707 Scientific Computer, Memory Expansion, Thesaurus Dictionary, Time and Expense Manager, Investment Planner, Bilingual and 8-Language Translators, Encyclopaedia of Wine, Spreadsheet (26 columns × 999 rows, Lotus 1-2-3 compatible), and games (Box Jockey/Sokoban, Tetris, Chess, Backgammon). A BASIC programming card arrived in 1991. Cards typically cost $50–120 each, making a fully-equipped Wizard a significant investment.

deepDive.heading: Seinfeld and Cultural Legacy
deepDive.text: In 'The Wizard' (Season 9, Episode 15, aired February 26, 1998), Jerry gives his father Morty a Sharp Wizard as a birthday present. Morty only ever uses it as a tip calculator. Elaine also buys one. The episode references a counterfeit knockoff brand called 'Willard' — organizers of poor quality bought cheap through 'Bob Sacamano's father.' The episode cemented the Wizard in American pop culture as a symbol of late-1990s tech aspiration (and chronic underuse), watched by tens of millions.

team.name: Sharp Corporation
team.note: Japanese electronics manufacturer founded by Tokuji Hayakawa. The Wizard was developed by Sharp's Electronic Organizer division, which later produced the Zaurus PDA line. No individual designer names have surfaced in public documentation.
